 Sameen Chaudhry, USA TODAY Updated Thu, November 12, 2026 at 2:56 PM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Patrick Desiato, who played bass and wrote songs for the Philadelphia rock band Cheer Up Dusty, has died. He was 36.
 His bandmates shared his Nov. 9 death, calling him their friend and brother in a Nov. 10 announcement on Instagram . They did not disclose a cause of death.
 "Pat was a creative mastermind, his influence on our band is not measurable," his bandmates wrote in an Instagram tribute . "Pat was our brain, he was our heart, he was every important organ you don't see when looking at a person but they need to function."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Desiato's family told his bandmates they played him "I Believe in You" as he was dying, the group wrote⁠. The song appeared on the band's 2021 release "EP 2: A Collection of Singles⁠." Desiato wrote and arranged the music for the entire EP and recorded every guitar and bass part.
 Bobby Taylor, beloved rock drummer, dies at 58 after cancer battle 
 "He was a soldier, a warrior. He was simply fantastic," the statement said. "The word love doesn't feel strong enough on how we feel about you Pat and what this all meant to us. Everything we do going forward will forever be for you."The bandmates thanked their fans for their love, support and prayers.
 Desiato helped write the 2022 single "Everybody Hates Me," which his bandmates called their biggest song. The track began as a demo by guitarist Brayan Marin, who told All the Alt Things ⁠ that Desiato initially doubted he could improvise a bass part. 
 Advertisement Advertisement "Pretty soon we figured out that Patty can jam and be creative on the fly," Marin said. 
 Sir Patrick Stewart, the award-winning actor known for starring in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises, died on Oct. 28 . He was 86.
Stewart's death was confirmed in a statement shared on his official social media accounts on Thursday, Oct. 29. The cause was Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement posted to his social media.
"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," the statement said.
Stewart was best known for his roles as Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and Charles Xavier in the "X-Men" movies. He is set to return as Professor Xavier in the upcoming Marvel film "Avengers: Doomsday." (David Livingston, Getty Images) John Frieda , the celebrity hairstylist and beauty entrepreneur behind the popular Frizz Ease hair care line, died in November 2026 at age 75. 
The British stylist worked with some of the biggest names in entertainment, including Princess Diana, Madonna, Nicole Kidman and Gwyneth Paltrow. 
Frieda launched Frizz Ease with business partner Gail Federici in 1988 and later introduced the Sheer Blonde line. In 2002, he sold his hair care company to Japanese conglomerate Kao in a deal valued at $450 million. 
He is survived by his wife, Frances Avery Agnelli, four children and two grandchildren. (LEON NEAL / AFP via Getty Images) Tony Butala , a founding member of the Grammy-nominated pop group The Lettermen, died Nov. 1 at age 87 in Manitowoc, Wisconsin, following several health issues, the group's manager, David Haskell, confirmed to USA TODAY.
Known for their signature three-part harmonies, The Lettermen rose to fame with renditions of classic songs including "The Way You Look Tonight," "When I Fall in Love" and "Goin' Out of My Head/Can't Take My Eyes Off You." 
Butala helped form the group in 1959 and remained a member until his retirement in 2019. The group continued touring with new singers, carrying on his musical legacy.
"He lived to be on stage," Haskell, a friend of Butala's for about 50 years, told USA TODAY. "He lived to bring people joy." (David Livingston / Getty Images) Barbara Barrie , the Oscar-nominated actress known for "Breaking Away" and "Suddenly Susan," died Oct. 28 at age 95 at her New York City home. 
Her agent, Gary Gersh, told USA TODAY that her death was medically assisted under New York's Medical Aid in Dying law. 
Barrie, who had been diagnosed with terminal cancer, previously disclosed a diagnosis of the incurable lung disease idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in 2014. 
Over her decades-long career, she earned Oscar, Tony and Emmy nominations, with credits including "Company," "Barney Miller" and "Private Benjamin." (Cindy Ord, Getty Images) German actress Elke Sommer , who starred opposite Peter Sellers in "A Shot in the Dark" from the Pink Panther series, died Oct. 28 at her home in Los Angeles' Bel Air neighborhood. She was 85.
Her stepson, Sebastian Walther, confirmed her death to the German outlet Bild, which reported that hse died of heart failure after an extended illness. "Elke passed away peacefully around 10 p.m. Now she can finally be with her beloved husband again," he told the outlet.
Sommer was one of Germany's best-known Hollywood stars in the 1960s, winning a Golden Globe for her performance opposite Paul Newman in "The Prize." Her other credits included "The Art of Love," "The Wrecking Crew" and "The Prisoner of Zenda," alongside work in TV and theater. (Express, Getty Images) Susan Saint James, the actress best known for her work opposite Rock Hudson on "McMillan & Wife" before finding sitcom success with "Kate & Allie," has died at 80. Her representative told People magazine⁠ that the actress died Oct. 26 after a battle with pancreatic cancer. 
Saint James built a television career that spanned crime dramas and comedies, receiving eight Emmy nominations⁠. She won in 1969 for her supporting performance in "The Name of the Game," with additional nominations for that series in 1970 and 1971⁠. (Charley Gallay/ Getty Images) Walter Koenig , the actor best known for playing Pavel Chekov on " Star Trek ," died Oct. 25 at his Los Angeles home, surrounded by his daughter and niece. He was 90.
His representative, Zachary McGinnis, confirmed to USA TODAY on Oct. 26 that he died of old age.
Koenig joined "Star Trek" in 1967 as the Enterprise's Russian navigator and reprised the role in the franchise's films. His other credits included "Babylon 5," "Columbo" and "Futurama," and he also worked as an author, theater director and acting teacher. (Alberto E. Rodriguez, Getty Images) Kevin Bleyer , an Emmy-winning writer on " The Daily Show " who previously wrote speeches for former President Barack Obama , died in a fatal car crash over the weekend. He was 54.
The Maryland native died Oct. 25 while driving on a rural road in Millrift, Pennsylvania, where he had a home, his family confirmed on Facebook Oct. 27. No one else was injured in the crash.
"Kevin spent his life finding the perfect words to make people laugh, think and see the world a little differently," his wife Nella Vera said in the statement. "I was lucky enough to know the humor, curiosity, mischief and tenderness behind those words — and to be loved by a man who made my own world more joyful, more adventurous and infinitely more beautiful." (Kevin Winter / Getty Images) Eric Bauza , the Emmy-winning voice actor who portrayed Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, and other cartoon favorites, died on Oct. 25 at age 45. His family announced his death on Instagram.
He died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease , according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner's Office report obtained by USA TODAY.
Bauza brought Looney Tunes characters to a new generation, earning three Children's & Family Emmys for his voice work. His credits also included Puss in Boots in "The Adventures of Puss in Boots," Baby Fozzie in "Muppet Babies" and roles in "Space Jam: A New Legacy" and "The Super Mario Bros. Movie." (Kevin Winter, Getty Images) Ryu Murakami , the Japanese novelist, artist and filmmaker, died Oct. 17 at his Tokyo home. He was 74; his longtime publisher, Gentosha, announced his death Oct. 23 without disclosing a cause.
Murakami was known for his provocative 1976 debut novel "Almost Transparent Blue" and books including "Audition," "Coin Locker Babies," and "In the Miso Soup." His dark fiction explored alienation, sex, drugs and violence, and several of his novels were adapted into films. (JIJI PRESS, JIJI PRESS/AFP via Getty Images) Michael Gray , the 1970s teen idol best known for playing Billy Batson in the CBS superhero series "Shazam!," died Oct. 16 of natural causes, his publicist confirmed Oct. 22. He was 75.
Gray rose to fame with appearances on "The Little People" and "The Brady Bunch" before starring in "Shazam!" from 1974 to 1976. He portrayed the teenager who transformed into Captain Marvel by shouting the superhero's name. 
After stepping away from Hollywood, Gray returned to acting in the 2016 comedy "Surge of Power: Revenge of the Sequel" and voiced a fictionalized version of himself on "Archer." He also made a cameo in the 2023 film "Shazam! Fury of the Gods." (Getty Images) Tom Skerritt , the Emmy-winning actor known for his roles in "M*A*S*H," "Alien," "Top Gun" and "Picket Fences," died Oct. 21 of natural causes, his family confirmed to USA TODAY. He was 93.
Skerritt's career spanned more than six decades. He broke through in Robert Altman's 1970 war comedy "M*A*S*H" before playing Dallas, captain of the Nostromo, in the 1979 science fiction classic "Alien." He later portrayed commanding officer Mike "Viper" Metcalf opposite Tom Cruise in 1986's "Top Gun." 
Skerritt won a 1993 Emmy for his role as Jimmy Brock on CBS' "Picket Fences." He continued acting into his 90s, appearing in the 2025 Western drama "Broke." (CHRIS DELMAS, AFP via Getty Images) John Anderson , the country singer and Country Music Hall of Fame member, died Oct. 21 at his home in Smithville, Tennessee, his team confirmed to The Tennessean , part of the USA TODAY Network. He was 71; the cause of death was not disclosed.
Anderson was known for his distinctive baritone and hits including "Swingin'," "Seminole Wind" and "Straight Tequila Night." His career took off in the early 1980s, and he was inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2014 and the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024. (Terry Wyatt, Getty Images) Richard Riehle , the versatile character actor best known for his roles in "Office Space" and "Grounded for Life," died at 78, according to a joint statement by his agency and management, which was shared with USA TODAY on Oct. 19.
Riehle, who had a master of fine arts degree from the University of Minnesota, racked up hundreds of film and TV credits across his five-decade career in Hollywood. The actor's talents spanned genres, with Riehle working in horror films, comedies, holiday movies and crime thrillers.
After his breakout role in Edward Zwick's 1989 Civil War epic "Glory," he appeared in "The Man from Earth," "Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo," "Free Willy" and "Casino," among other movies. He also had TV roles on "Barry," The Young and the Restless" and several "Star Trek" series. (Fox Broadcasting) Sahara Ray (center) has died at 34 years old. The Australian model, who was once romantically linked to celebrities like Justin Bieber and Cody Simpson, died over the weekend, her family told TMZ in a statement on Monday, Oct. 19. A cause of death was not revealed.
The swimwear brand founder was the daughter of Australian surfer Tony Ray and rose to fame as a model and influencer. In 2024, Ray revealed to her followers that she was living with Guillain-Barré syndrome , a rare autoimmune condition. (Frazer Harrison, Getty Images for Ashton Michael) Longtime NPR personality Noah Adams, right, died Oct. 16 at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio, wife Neenah Ellis told the radio broadcaster . He was 84.
As a host for "All Things Considered" from 1982 to 1987 and 1989 to 2002, the writer and storyteller covered the fall of the Berlin Wall, 9/11 and human-focused stories in rural communities across the country. His former colleagues highlighted Adams' 1981 radio documentary " Father Cares: The Last of Jonestown " as one of his standout works. (Tim Dillon/USA TODAY) RJ Mitte , the "Breaking Bad" actor who advocated for disability rights throughout his career, died at 34 on Oct. 12. 
Mitte, who played Walter White Jr. on the Emmy-winning AMC drama series, was declared dead at 1:32 p.m. local time at his residence in Brownsville, Texas, Cameron County Justice of the Peace Judge Cyndi Hinojosa told USA TODAY. The actor's rep Sean Reilly also confirmed his death in a statement, describing Mitte as a "beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate." (Hatnim Lee, Getty Images) Lucian Piane , the Grammy-nominated music producer, composer and "RuPaul's Drag Race" guest judge, died Oct. 12 at 46. He died after being struck by a car, according to TMZ, which cited the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner.
Piane was known for composing the themes for "RuPaul's Drag Race" and "RuPaul's Drag U," helping contestants with musical challenges and producing RuPaul's albums "Champion," "Glamazon" and "Born Naked."
He also co-wrote Sia's "Free Me" and released satirical remixes under the name RevoLucian. (Imeh Akpanudosen, Getty Images for MTV) TV personality Amber Siyavus , a former " Big Brother " contestant, died Oct. 9 in Clark County, Nevada. She was 46, according to coroner records USA TODAY reviewed. Her cause and manner of death were pending.
Siyavus famously competed on Season of the CBS reality series in 2007. When she joined the cast as a Las Vegas server, she spent more than 60 days in the house and frequently spoke about her daughter, Lexi. (Kevin Winter, Getty Images for Fox) Michael Kearns , an actor who broke barriers when he publicly shared his HIV status in 1991, has died at 76, the Celebration Theatre in Santa Monica, California, shared on Oct. 6.
Kearns, who served as the theater's artistic director from 1986 to 1987, was set to perform selections from Robert Chesley’s 1986 play "Jerker," a story he directed that centers on two gay men falling in love over a phone-sex line in the early years of the AIDS epidemic.
"Michael's legacy in theaters, in performances, in wherever he went and touched, including our hearts, is unparalleled," his friend, Roland Palencia, wrote in an Oct. 7 tribute . "All I know is that where his soul travels, it will be a much more interesting place, by far, ever!" (Valerie Macon, Getty Images) Jim Bakker (pictured right), the televangelist whose broadcasting empire collapsed amid a sex scandal and fraud conviction, died Oct. 5 at 86.
His wife, Lori Bakker, announced his death on his official Instagram account. She did not disclose a cause of death.
Bakker founded PTL ministries and built a Christian television empire alongside his then-wife, Tammy Faye Bakker (pictured left). His career unraveled in the late 1980s, and he served nearly five years in prison after being convicted on 24 federal counts of fraud and conspiracy tied to his ministry's fundraising practices. (SCOTT MILIMAN, AFP via Getty Images) Anika Rashaun , a reality TV personality and dating coach, died at 34 after being diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer. Her friend and podcast cohost Tiara Ramos announced her death in an Oct. 5 Substack post; an exact date of death wasn't disclosed.
Rashaun was known for appearing on MTV's "Real World Seattle: Bad Blood" in 2016 and "The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions" in 2017. She later became a matchmaker and cohosted the podcast "Breast Friends Forever," launched after her cancer diagnosis. (Stephanie Girard) Niamh O'Brien, a "Lord of the Dance" performer, died Oct. 5 at 52. 
"My heart is broken. I have lost my beautiful wife, Niamh, and my best friend," American-Irish choreographer Michael Flatley wrote in an Oct. 5 Instagram tribute ⁠. "My gorgeous bride of twenty years has gone to the Lord in Heaven. She was the most loving mother, wife and person, and our lives will never be the same without her."
 The Irish Times reported ⁠ that O'Brien had a longstanding lung condition that worsened over the past year. She had been scheduled to travel to the United States for a lung transplant but died before the procedure. (ShowBizIreland, Getty Images) "North by Northwest" star Eva Marie Saint died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles on Oct. 6, her representative, Jeff Sanderson, confirmed to USA TODAY. 
Ahead of her death at age 102, the blonde starlet was the oldest living Oscar winner, awarded in the supporting actress category at the 1955 Academy Awards for her work in "On the Waterfront."
Saint was also known for films like "Because of Winn-Dixie" (2005) and "Superman Returns" (2006), as well as several TV shows, from "How the West Was Won" to "Moonlighting." She was nominated for five Emmys but won on her fifth nod in 1990 for playing Lil Altemus on "People Like Us."
 (Neilson Barnard, Getty Images) Jeffrey Archer , the bestselling British novelist behind "Kane and Abel" and the "Clifton Chronicles," died at 86 at his home on Oct. 5.
His publisher HarperCollins said in a statement ⁠ that Archer died "suddenly and peacefully" while "between writing sessions." He died a day before the scheduled Oct. 6 release of "Adam & Eve," which he planned as his final novel. (Joseph Okpako/ Getty Images) Freddie Jackson , the R&B singer best known for the '80s hits " Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake) " and " You Are My Lady ," died days after his birthday, his family announced on Oct. 6. He was 67.
"Freddie was more than a legendary voice. He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends, and his music with everything he had," his family wrote on Instagram. 
 (Astrid Stawiarz, Getty Images) Sass Jordan , the Juno-winning rock singer-songwriter and former "Canadian Idol" judge, died Oct. 2 surrounded by her family, according to a statement shared on her Instagram account. She was 65. A cause of death has not been disclosed.
Jordan was known for her powerhouse vocals and songs, including "Tell Somebody" and "Make You a Believer." Her 1988 debut album earned her a Juno Award for most promising female vocalist, and she later served as a judge on all six seasons of "Canadian Idol." (WILLIAM HAMES, PROVIDED BY IMPACT RECORDS) Conrad "Cronus" Lant , bassist and frontman of the British heavy metal band Venom, died aged 63 on Oct. 1, his band announced in a social media post. A cause of death was not provided.
Lant was known for the voice, bass playing and vision that helped shape Venom's sound. He appeared on landmark albums like "Welcome to Hell" and "Black Metal" and remained the band's most consistent member across more than four decades. (Jo Hale, Getty Images) Dennis Haskins , the actor best known for playing lovable principal Richard Belding on the NBC teen sitcom " Saved by the Bell, " died at 75. Haskins' agent, Jay Schachter, confirmed the actor's death to USA TODAY on Sept. 29. A cause of death was not immediately announced.
Haskins became an instantly recognizable TV presence as Bayside High's well-meaning principal who was frequently comically exasperated by the schemes of Zack Morris (Mark-Paul Gosselaar) and his friends.
 (Michael Kovac, Getty Images for Festival of Art) Singer-songwriter Slinger Francisco, better known by his stage name Mighty Sparrow, died on Sept. 27 at the age of 91 following a brief illness, Francisco's family confirmed to The Associated Press .
Francisco helped popularize the Calypso genre, a Caribbean style known for its fast rhythms and harmonic vocals. Dubbed the "Calypso King of the World," the singer is best known for his 1956 hit "Jean and Dinah." 
 (Tim Shaffer, Reuters) Angela Stribling , a radio personality and former BET host, died on Sept. 26 at the age of 58 following a battle with brain cancer, Stribling's husband, Ken Washington, shared in an Instagram post.
The New York-born TV personality and singer hosted BET's entertainment news show "Screen Scene" in the 1990s and pioneered the network's jazz coverage by hosting "Jazz Central" and other programs.
 (Paul Morigi) Gary "Angry" Anderson , the gravel-voiced frontman of Australian hard rock band Rose Tattoo, died on Sept. 21 at the age of 79, according to a joint statement shared by his family and the band. A cause of death was not disclosed, although Anderson was recently hospitalized after suffering cardiac arrest while Rose Tattoo was touring in Germany, according to The Guardian . 
The singer spent five decades as the frontman of Rose Tattoo, which formed in Sydney in 1976⁠. The band established itself as a fixture of Australian hard rock with songs including "Bad Boy for Love," "Rock 'n' Roll Outlaw," "We Can't Be Beaten" and "Nice Boys." 
 (Lisa Maree Williams/ Getty Images) Chad Gilbert , the longtime New Found Glory guitarist, died on Sept. 20 at the age of 45, according to a joint statement from his wife, Lisa Cimorelli, and his bandmates. A cause of death was not disclosed, but Gilbert had been documenting his yearslong battle with a rare cancer since 2021.
Gilbert was one of the founding members of New Found Glory, a hardcore punk band known for hits such as "All Downhill From Here," "Dressed to Kill" and "Hit or Miss."
 (Bryan Bedder, Getty Images) Presley Gerber , the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, died Sept. 20 at 27, Crawford's representative confirmed to USA TODAY. Presley, who signed with IMG Models in his teens, died at a rehab facility, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records.
 He appeared on the runway and in ad campaigns for fashion brands such as Tommy Hilfiger, Moschino, Balmain and more.
 (Frazer Harrison, Getty Images) Duncan Sheik , the Grammy- and Tony-winning singer-songwriter and composer, died of organ failure on Thursday, Sept. 17, at a Manhattan hospital, his mother confirmed to the New York Times. He was 56.
Sheik was best known for "Barely Breathing," his 1996 breakout hit, and for composing music for Broadway's "Spring Awakening." The musical won eight Tonys in 2007, with Sheik taking home awards for best original score and best orchestrations.
 (Rob Kim, Getty Images) British rapper Sway DaSafo , who made history as the first unsigned artist to win Best Hip-Hop Act at the MOBO Awards, has died at age 44. His death was announced Thursday, Sept. 17, by the MOBO Awards. 
Born Derek Safo in North London to Ghanaian parents, DaSafo released five studio albums and two EPs during his decades-long career. His 2006 single "Little Derek" reached No. 30 on the U.K. Singles Chart and appeared on his debut album, "This Is My Demo." He also collaborated with Akon and appeared in "Top Boy" and "The Grind."
 (LEON NEAL, AFP via Getty Images) Gerrit Graham (far left), the distinctive character actor, screenwriter and songwriter known for his decadeslong career in showbiz, died of complications with lung disease on Sept. 15, his family confirmed. He was 77.
Graham was best known for playing the ill-fated glam-rock star Beef in Brian De Palma's "Phantom of the Paradise," as well as roles in "Pretty Baby," "Used Cars" and "Child's Play 2." 
He also cowrote the Grateful Dead song "Victim or the Crime" with Bob Weir.
 (Carlos Alvarez, Getty Images) Bob Mackie , the legendary Emmy- and Tony-winning fashion and costume designer, died on Sept. 14 at the age of 87, the designer's team shared in an Instagram statement. A cause of death was not disclosed.
Mackie was famous for his signature embellished and beaded fashion and costume designs for Cher, Carol Burnett, Dolly Parton, Tina Turner, Diana Ross, Liza Minnelli and more.
 (Craig Barritt, Getty Images for Cunard) Pete Byrne , half of the 1980s new wave duo Naked Eyes, died on Sept. 14 at the age of 74 following a brief illness, the band's team announced on its official website.
Byrne, with the late keyboardist and songwriter Rob Fisher, founded Naked Eyes in 1982. The synth-pop group went on to release a number of hits, including the Billboard Top 10 singles "Always Something There to Remind Me" (a cover of the Burt Bacharach and Hal David track originally sung by Dionne Warwick) and "Promises, Promises."
 (Ron Wolfson, Michael Ochs Archives via Getty Images) Peter Max , the artist best known for his colorful, psychedelic paintings that became synonymous with the flower power movement in the 1960s, has died at 88. Max, who was living with dementia for at least a decade, died in a hospital on Sept. 14, his son Adam Max told The New York Times and The Associated Press on Sept. 16.
During his career, he met several presidents, saw his design welcoming visitors to the United States displayed at the Canadian and Mexican borders, appeared on the cover of Life magazine in 1969, and became known for his "Cosmic '60s" posters.
 (Tim Boyle/Newsmakers via Getty Images) Cheetah Chrome , the influential guitarist who helped shape punk rock as a member of the Dead Boys and Rocket from the Tombs, has died at the age of 71, the Dead Boys announced in an Instagram tribute⁠ on Sept. 13. A cause of death was not disclosed. 
Born Eugene Richard O'Connor, Chrome joined the proto-punk band Rocket from the Tombs in 1974, followed by the Dead Boys in 1975. Dead Boys, known for their seminal debut album "Young, Loud and Snotty," became fixtures at CBGB, the Manhattan club that served as a launching pad for some of punk's most influential acts.
 (Theo Wargo/ Getty Images) Jon Small , the music video director, producer and longtime collaborator of Billy Joel , has died. Joel confirmed Small's death in a brief Instagram post on Sept. 7. "RIP Jon Small," the hitmaker captioned photos of the pair.
Small played with Joel in the 1970s bands the Hassles and Attila before they fell out over Joel's affair with Small's wife. The pair later reconciled, with Small going on to directed music videos for the "Piano Man" singer as well as Reba McEntire, Luther Vandross, Run-DMC, Garth Brooks, Enrique Iglesias, Blake Shelton and more.
 (Andrew H. Walker) Grammy Award-winning jazz musician Cassandra Wilson died in her hometown of Jackson, Mississippi, on Sept. 2, her manager told radio station WBGO . She was 70.
The genre-bending singer, who infused elements of blues, country and folk into her music, won Grammys for Best Jazz Vocal Performance for 1995's "New Moon Daughter" and Best Jazz Vocal Album for 2008's "Loverly." 
In 2022, she was awarded the National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Masters Fellowship, the nation's highest honor for jazz artists.
 (Theo Wargo) Wendell Berry (pictured left), the novelist, poet, farmer and influential environmentalist whose work championed rural life, died at his Port Royal, Kentucky, home on Aug. 31. He was 92.
Berry, whose cause of death was not disclosed, was known for writing about farming, community and the costs of industrialization. His honors included the National Humanities Medal in 2012 and induction into the Kentucky Writers' Hall of Fame in 2015.
 (Mark Wilson, Getty Images) Peter Cullen , the Canadian voice actor who gave life to Optimus Prime across "Transformers" films, TV and video-game projects, died Aug. 26 at his Los Angeles home, his agent, Kevin Motley, confirmed to USA TODAY. He was 85.
"Peter Cullen passed away peacefully, surrounded by his loving family – and held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide," his family said in a statement. TMZ later reported that his cause of death was cardiac arrest due to respiratory arrest, as listed on his death certificate.
Cullen was best known as the leader of the Autobots, as well as Eeyore in numerous "Winnie the Pooh" projects. His decades-long voice-acting career also includes "Voltron," "Knight Rider," "Predator," and more.
 (ANGELA WEISS, AFP via Getty Images) Yayoi Kusama , the Japanese avant-garde artist behind some of contemporary art's most recognizable images and installations, died Aug. 14 at a Tokyo hospital, according to a statement by the Yayoi Kusama Museum.
The museum said Kusama, who died aged 97, continued painting until her final days.
Kusama was known for her signature polka dots, pumpkin sculptures and immersive "Infinity Mirror Rooms," as well as a boundary-pushing career across painting, sculpture, performance, literature and poetry.
 (Mike Segar, REUTERS) Tim Curry , the actor celebrated for his roles as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic film " The Rocky Horror Picture Show " and Pennywise the Clown in the 1990 version of "It," died Aug. 25 at 80. Curry's longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz confirmed the news in a statement shared by rep Sean Katz.
Curry had been suffering from health issues in recent years and continued to struggle with mobility after a 2012 stroke.
 (Alberto E. Rodriguez, Getty Images) Dolly Parton , the beloved, groundbreaking country music singer, actor and philanthropist, died Aug. 25 at 80. The award-winning "Jolene" singer's death was confirmed in a social media message shared by her nephew, Bryan Seaver . "She will always love you," he said.
The cultural icon died in a Nashville cancer center surrounded by loved ones after briefly  battling cancer , her representatives confirmed to USA TODAY.
 (David Becker, Getty Images) Singer, actress and TV personality Jaye P. Morgan died at age 94 of natural causes on Aug. 24, her representatives confirmed to USA TODAY. 
The entertainer was known for hit recordings in the 1950s, including "Life Is Just a Bowl of Cherries," as well as several TV appearances, including her memorable stint as a celebrity panelist on "The Gong Show."
 (Courtesty of Jaye P. Morgan) Shelley Fabares , best known for "The Donna Reed Show" and "Coach," died Aug. 22 at 82.
Fabares' family confirmed her death to People magazine , remembering the actress whose "work became part of the fabric of American television and film."
Fabares earned her most famous role as the beloved daughter of Donna Reed's character, Mary, on the 1960s hit sitcom. She went on to have a brief music career, with the hit single "Johnny Angel," star in multiple films opposite Elvis Presley and appear on the TV shows "One Day at a Time," "Highway to Heaven," "Little House on the Prairie" and "Coach," the latter opposite Craig T. Nelson.
 (Carlo Allegri, Getty Images) James Lew , a veteran stunt performer, coordinator and actor whose credits spanned decades of film and TV, died Aug. 23 at 73.
His wife, Jordana Potter, announced his death in a touching Instagram tribute .
"Honey I imagine you walking the beach with Dudley, sparring with Bruce Lee and finally getting to hug your Dad again," she wrote. "James MF Lew you are loved and will be deeply missed."
Lew was known for his work on "Big Trouble in Little China," "They Live," "Escape From L.A." and the "Rush Hour" films, plus his comedic fight scene in "Hot Shots! Part Deaux." He won an Emmy in 2017 for stunt coordination on Netflix's "Luke Cage."
 (Frazer Harrison, Getty Images) Music manager Dale Morris , who guided the careers of country stars Kenny Chesney and Alabama, died on Aug. 21, his management firm, Morris Higham Management, announced on social media. He was 89. Morris' family said in a news release that he died in his sleep.
Morris' client Chesney went on to become one of country music's most enduring stars following his 1994 debut. With Morris' help, the singer scored a string of over 20 No. 1 country hits and four consecutive entertainer of the year awards at the Academy of Country Music Awards.
 (Morris Highham Management) Actor Michael Wright , pictured center, died on Aug. 19, his wife, Susan Wright, confirmed on social media.
